why: R1-R18, the writing style this repo enforces: make the WORK the subject, or use the
shared 'we'. Never 'you', never 'I'. This file is the single source of truth for the
rules; .ci/rediacc_ci/quality/prose_style.py reads it and holds no rule text of its own.
WHY JSON AND NOT YAML, which the brief asked for first. PyYAML is NOT importable by the
interpreter that runs this repo's pytest suite. Measured 2026-09-16:
$ .ci/cache/toolchain/uv-tools/pytest/bin/python -c 'import yaml'
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'
pytest is provisioned by `uv tool install`, which builds an ISOLATED virtual environment,
so the system interpreter's PyYAML 6.0.3 is not on its path. .ci/rediacc_ci/workflows.py
records the same constraint and paid for it with a hand-written YAML subset parser. A
rules file this gate's own tests cannot load is a gate that cannot be tested, so the
format is JSON, which every interpreter here reads from the standard library.
EVERY RULE CARRIES ITS EXAMPLES, and the examples ARE the test fixtures:
.ci/rediacc_ci/tests/test_quality_prose_style.py generates one case per example. An
example with no expectation would be decoration, so each one states what must happen:
flag        at least one rule must fire on it, and when the OWNING rule carries
patterns, the owning rule must be among those that fire -- unless the
example names a `caught_by`, which is then the rule that must fire
caught_by   the rule that REALLY catches this example, when it is not the rule the
example belongs to. R11's `Your feedback...` is a hidden-you, which is
R11's subject, but the word `your` is R1's pattern and R11 has no reason
to carry a second copy of it. Recording that is better than either
duplicating the pattern or weakening the assertion to `something fired`,
which is how an example comes to rely on a neighbouring rule silently.
clean       no rule may fire on it
undetected  beyond mechanical detection, and SAID SO rather than quietly dropped.
Asserted NOT to fire, and counted in the gate's shape line, so the
coverage gap is visible in every run instead of living in this comment.
THE `undetected` ROWS ARE THE HONEST PART. R12's 'The project failed.' and R3's good
example 'The build failed after the last change.' are the SAME surface shape, and telling
them apart needs to know whether the subject is a project or a build. A pattern that
flagged one would flag the other, so neither is flagged and this file says why.
SEVERITY: `error` exits non-zero, `warning` prints and does not. SCOPES name where a rule
applies; `all` is every scope. A scope a rule does not list is a place the rule is not
checked, which is how R11's imperative arm stays out of code comments and commit subjects.

reason: BLOCKER: live per-session coordination scratch, written continuously by running
sessions. A CI gate that reds because a CONCURRENT session wrote a 430-character
line in its own notes is failing for a reason unrelated to the commit under test,
which is flakiness wearing a gate's name. Measured 2026-09-16: 10 of the tracked
STATE.md files already carry over-length lines, and the two that triggered this
entry belong to the session that dispatched the work, so they were not this

exempt_paths.reason: BLOCKER: the archived copies of the same scratch, kept as a record. Rewriting a record to satisfy a line-length rule would falsify the record.

reason: BLOCKER: a GENERATED artifact, not authored prose. `worklist.py --publish` renders
this file from the append-only worklist event log, so every line in it is the text
of a worklist item, and most of those items belong to sessions that have ended. The
four R2 findings that triggered this entry (#043041d3, #0d972047, #1e5ce54d,
#2e642173) were all written by f4da5c2e and are ticked and closed; the only way to
clear them at the artifact is to rewrite a dead session's history in an
append-only store. check_plan_citations.py settled the same scope question for the
same tree and the same reason: `agent/pr/*.md, agent/worklist/*   OUT. Generated.
The fix for a dead pointer in a generated file is a change to the generator, and
reporting it at the artifact teaches the wrong lesson.` Prose style in a rendered
snapshot of historical items is that case exactly. The generator, and the style of
items written from here on, remain in scope through the source files themselves.

exempt_why: EXEMPT IS NOT EXCLUDED, and the difference is the whole point. An `exclude_dirs` entry
leaves no trace; an `exempt_paths` entry is COUNTED and PRINTED on every run, so the
debt cannot be forgotten and a growing exemption list is visible in the shape line
rather than discoverable only by reading this file.
Every entry carries a `BLOCKER:` reason, the same convention
docs/agent-reference/suppressions.md requires of every other allowlist in this tree.
`agent/PLAN-*.md` is deliberately NOT here: it is an authored document that a
person reads, which is exactly what this style is for. `agent/pr/*.md` WAS here
until it turned out to be generated, not authored -- see its own entry above.
exclude_why: private/ holds four GIT SUBMODULES (account, elite, homebrew-tap, renet), which are
separate repositories. Measured 2026-09-16: they carried 27,015 of the 38,040 findings
on the first full sweep, 71 percent of the total, and not one of those files is this
repository's to rewrite. A gate whose baseline is mostly another repo's debt reports on
packages/www is out of scope for this pass: 217 translated, hash-pinned marketing files
whose English is the source of 12 derived locales, so a reflow there re-keys the i18n
naturalization ledger. .sh is absent from `include` on purpose and not by oversight:
shell scripts are a shrinking surface under this repo's bash-to-Python migration, and
teaching this tool a comment syntax it will outlive is effort spent backwards.
exclude_dirs now only describes TRACKED directories that are out of scope. discover()
enumerates `git ls-files`, so a gitignored or never-added path is excluded structurally
and needs no entry here. `.claude/hooks/context/state` was one such entry, added after
944aa6210 froze six of its ignored files into this gate's committed baseline; it is gone
because the corpus itself is now git's answer rather than the walking machine's.

rules.title: No "you"
rules.description: The words you, your, yours and yourself are not used to address the reader. The work becomes the subject instead.

rules.title: No "I"
rules.description: The words I, me, my, mine and myself are not used, nor the openers "Let me" and "I'll". A short ownership of one's own mistake is the one exception, and even there the word "I" stays out.
exceptions_why: `I/O`, `i18n` and `i.e.` are not the pronoun, and a gate that flagged them would be
deleted within a week. Roman numerals are admitted only behind a noun that takes one
(`Phase I`), never bare: a bare capital I in running prose IS the pronoun.

examples.text: My mistake; the fix is on the way.

rules.title: Passive and state structures
rules.description: Agentless passive, modal passive, get-passive, need + -ing, "is yet to be", and ergative verbs are the preferred ways to say what happened without naming who.

examples.text: Could the file be sent over today?
The contract is yet to be signed.
The build failed after the last change.

rules.title: Impersonal frames
rules.description: "It...", "There...", and seem/appear move the sentence off a person and onto the situation.

examples.text: It might be worth checking again.
Was there a chance to look at the proposal?
The file appears to be missing.

rules.title: Focus on the work and its state
rules.description: Nominalization, status adjectives (ready, pending, due, outstanding), verbless questions, gerund subjects and wh-clefts all put the artifact where the person was.

examples.text: Sending the file today would help.
What would help is a short summary.

rules.title: Shared "we"
rules.description: "We" and "Let's" are allowed, for shared work. They are not used to spread the blame for one's own mistake.

examples.text: Let's see how we can fix this.
We could take another look at the schema together.

rules.title: Hedging
rules.description: Could, might, would, perhaps, maybe and possibly carry a claim better than an absolute does. Absolutes are flagged.
patterns_why: THE BARE WORDS `never` AND `always` WERE THE FIRST CUT, AND THEY DID NOT
DISCRIMINATE. Measured on this tree 2026-09-16: R7 produced 7,710 of the 10,944
findings in the initial baseline, 70 percent of the total, and a warning that fires
on seven of every ten findings is noise by construction rather than a signal.
Reading the matches says why. In this repository `never` and `always` are how an
INVARIANT is stated -- 'never hand-edit this file', 'an entry without paths is ALWAYS
selected', 'the ADDED side must be empty, never merely smaller'. That is a
specification, and a specification is supposed to be absolute. R7 is about an
unhedged CLAIM ABOUT THE FUTURE, which is what its own bad example is: 'That will
never work.'
So the two words are anchored behind a MODAL, which is the grammar that turns a
description into a prediction. `will never work` and `can never fire` fire; `never
hand-edit this file` and `a gate that never fires` do not.
COPULAS WERE IN THE ANCHOR FOR ONE ROUND AND CAME BACK OUT, on evidence from the same
sweep. `was never bash` is a statement of fact about the past and `an entry without
paths is ALWAYS selected` is a specification; neither is an unhedged claim about what
will happen, which is what R7's own bad example is. A modal is the only form that
reliably marks the difference.
`certainly` left the list at the same time: its common use here is concessive ('this
is certainly slower, and correct'), which is hedging rather than the absence of it.

examples.text: This may not work as expected; worth testing first.

rules.title: No flattery
rules.description: Praise goes to the work, not to the person. Opening a reply by complimenting the asker is the shape this refuses.

examples.text: The project came together really well.

rules.title: Thanks are welcome, not flattering
rules.description: Thanking is not flattery. Thanks are said in full, and directed at what the help produced.

examples.text: Thanks to Mark for his help on this.

rules.title: Group address when criticizing
rules.description: No names are used in criticism. A group reminder carries the same information without pointing.
detection_why: Naming a person is only a defect when the sentence is CRITICAL, and no pattern
separates 'Ahmet reviewed the schema' from 'Ahmet always gossips'. A name detector
would flag every attribution line in the repository, including the ones R9 asks for.

examples.text: Gossip can really hurt a team.
Just a reminder for everyone: timesheets are due Friday.

rules.title: Hidden "you"
rules.description: An imperative in a request or a piece of feedback addresses the reader without the word. So does "your", and so does the generic "you".
exempt_scopes_why: `comment` is absent because an imperative code comment ('Return early if empty') is the
house idiom and addresses nobody. `commit` is absent because this repository's commit
subjects are Conventional-Commits-shaped and frequently imperative by convention;
measured over the last 200 commits, median 71 characters, p90 84, max 98. The brief's
own text exempts both, and compatibility with the conventions already in the tree wins.

rules.title: Softer wording
rules.description: A blunt verdict about an outcome reads as a verdict about whoever produced it. The same fact lands better as a state to look into.
detection_why: 'The project failed.' and R3's good example 'The build failed after the last change.'
are the same surface shape. Separating them needs to know what kind of noun the
subject is, so neither is flagged and the gap is declared instead of guessed at.

examples.text: The project didn't work out as planned.
This is something to look into.

rules.title: Make things easier and give good news
rules.description: A cost is reported with its path forward attached, rather than as a closed door.

examples.text: This will take some time, but it's doable.

rules.title: Soft refusal
rules.description: A refusal names the constraint, or names a better route, rather than the speaker's willingness.

examples.text: Unfortunately that won't be possible this week.
Maria might be the best person for this.

rules.title: Leave the argument
rules.description: Repeating a point louder, or dismissing it, both keep the argument going. Another wording, or a pause, ends it.

examples.text: Here's another way to put it.
Let's leave it there for now and revisit later.

rules.title: Euphemism for private matters
rules.description: A private matter is reported at the level of its effect on the work, not in its details.
detection_why: Detecting this would mean a medical-vocabulary list, which is both unbounded and the
wrong instrument: 'He has a stomach bug' is a defect and 'the stomach bug fix landed'
is not, and only the surrounding sentence knows which.

rules.title: Keep the balance
rules.description: The passive is not used to hide responsibility for one's own mistake. Heavy passive throughout a passage is flagged on the same grounds.

examples.text: My error; a fix is on the way.

rules.title: Line length
rules.description: Prose lines stay at or under about 384 characters. Paragraphs are not hard-wrapped at any narrower width, which is what the reflow subcommand exists to undo.
detection_why: Length is counted, not matched, so this rule carries no regex. The limit lives in
`globals.max_line_length` because the reflow subcommand needs the same number and two
copies of a width is how a reflow starts producing lines its own linter refuses.

examples.text: A line well under the limit.
